claims.text: Creating a multi-principal-element alloy introduces a high-entropy effect.
The high-entropy effect can stabilize near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals.
High configurational entropy lowers the Gibbs free energy of the solid solution.
Lowering the solid solution's Gibbs free energy stabilizes the host matrix against sintering.
The proposed intervention protects the nanoparticles against structural or chemical instability.
The proposed stabilization applies throughout the 773–1173 K catalytic regime.
Nanoparticles with the high-entropy effect will be more stable and sinter less than otherwise identical nanoparticles without the effect.
The starting material is crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of at least five metals.
The hypothesis is bounded to continuous operation but does not specify a numerical exposure duration.
Successful stabilization may require careful control of alloy composition and processing conditions.
The exact stabilization mechanism and the limitations of the intervention are uncertain.
XRD, TEM, XPS, and catalytic-activity measurements can be used to evaluate the exposed nanoparticles.
Observation of significant sintering or structural or chemical instability in the intervened nanoparticles would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The starting nanoparticles are already near-equiatomic alloys containing five or more principal metals, while the intervention is defined as creating a multi-principal-element alloy to introduce high entropy. Thus, the intervention does not specify a distinct change from the initial state, and a same-composition baseline 'without the high-entropy effect' is not operationally defined.
